In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of mineral indicators for two different sedimentary environments in the Tertiary–Holocene sequence of the Grand Banks.
the use of clay minerals as indicators of the geochemical and geological modification of sediments in the near-surface environment.

the identification and description of the clay mineral assemblages in sediments of different ages, and the application of these assemblages to the study of the sedimentary environment and the history of sea level changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
(1) The Tertiary sediments in the study area were deposited under normal marine conditions, with some evidence of a regressive phase.
the sediments of the study area are characterized by two major sedimentary units: a weathered, acid-leached zone and a deeper zone of alkaline marine sediments.

the sediments on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland are characterized by a complex history of deposition and diagenetic alteration, which has led to the formation of a number of different clay mineral suites, which in turn are controlled by a number of different factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the clay mineralogy of the Tertiary sedimens on the northeastern Grand Bank is indicative of a complex geological history.
the Tertiary sedimens of the Grand Banks are not as homogeneous as was thought before and the clay mineral distribution pattern is not as simple as was expected.
the mineralogy of the < 2-μm clay-sized fraction is an effective indicator of the subaerial weathering history of sediments in this area.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Tertiary–Pleistocene boundary is a major discontinuity on the Grand Banks.
the Tertiary–Holocene sediment sequence in the study area is a complex, heterogeneous assemblage of sedimentary environments.
